filename: Investigating Western North America Atmospheric Rivers with Machine Learning-Based Detection.pdf
title: Investigating Western North America Atmospheric Rivers with Machine Learning-Based Detection
testbed_rationale: This study focuses on extreme event segmentation and tracking (atmospheric rivers) using a pre-existing CNN architecture (CGNet), rather than developing or benchmarking ML parameterizations or emulators for climate models.
pain_points: Spatial resolution mismatch: CGNet performance degrades significantly if input data (e.g., MERRA-2 at 0.5°) is not regridded to the training resolution (0.25°).
Sensitivity to input normalization under climate change: using historical vs. future warming normalization parameters shifts detected AR frequency by >15% due to mean-state moisture increases.

Data availability and missing diagnostics: high-frequency (3-hourly) total precipitable water (TMQ) was not standard in historical/future CESM runs, necessitating estimation from PS and Q, or temporal interpolation from 6-hourly data.
Severe class imbalance: the overwhelming dominance of the background class over ARs and TCs complicates training and depresses mean IoU.
Limited expert-labeled training samples: only 459 labeled images spanning 219 time steps were available from ClimateNet, limiting the diversity of synoptic states sampled.
extraction_notes: The paper uses CGNet for offline semantic segmentation and connected-component tracking of atmospheric rivers on CESM1.3 simulation output and reanalyses.
